title: Real Consumer Spending Fell in October While Prices Rose 3.8 Percent: Run Price Volume Mix Analysis by Entity From the Books, Put a Volume Line in the 2027 Revenue Budget, and Explain November Before the Board Asks
excerpt: The Bureau of Economic Analysis reported on November 25, 2026 that consumer spending rose 0.3 percent in October while prices rose 0.3 percent, so real spending fell, and the PCE price index is up 3.8 percent over the year. Here is how to run price volume mix analysis by entity from invoice lines in the books, what the three effects said about one three-entity group's October, how to rebuild the 2027 revenue budget as units times price, and how to write the November variance before the board asks.
author: FinBoard Team
coverAlt: CFO's worksheet for price volume mix analysis after the October 2026 Personal Income and Outlays release, showing three entities' revenue bridges split into price, volume, and mix effects, the 2027 budget volume line, and the November variance for the board
content:
Real consumer spending fell in October while prices rose 3.8 percent, so a revenue line that grew 3 percent may hold no new units. Run price volume mix analysis by entity from invoice lines in the books, give the 2027 revenue budget an explicit volume line, and explain November's variance as price, volume, and mix before the board asks.

Why price volume mix analysis matters now

The Bureau of Economic Analysis released Personal Income and Outlays, October 2026 on 2026-11-25. Current-dollar consumer spending rose $63.8 billion, or 0.3 percent, with $11.8 billion of that in goods and $52.1 billion in services. The PCE price index also rose 0.3 percent in the month and 3.8 percent from a year earlier, 3.3 percent excluding food and energy. Strip the price change out and real spending fell $5.8 billion, a decline the release rounds to less than 0.1 percent. Personal income rose 0.7 percent, disposable income 0.8 percent, and the saving rate was 4.1 percent. The next release, for November, is scheduled for December 23, 2026.

The same morning BEA published its second estimate of third-quarter GDP, also dated 2026-11-25: growth of 4.3 percent at an annual rate, revised up from 3.4 percent, 'primarily reflecting upward revisions to investment and consumer spending,' with the PCE price index for the quarter at 2.1 percent. So the quarter that just closed was strong in volume, and the first month of the new quarter was not. That is the shape of a demand turn, and it is the shape most 2027 revenue budgets were not built for.

The policy side is already moving. The minutes of the October 27 to 28 FOMC meeting, released 2026-11-18, show the committee held the target range at 3.75 to 4 percent on a 10 to 2 vote, with two members preferring a quarter-point increase, 'almost all' participants expecting further tightening, and some suggesting 'an increase of more than 25 basis points could warrant consideration' if inflation data proved unfavorable. The next meeting is December 8 to 9. CNBC's report on the release, published 2026-11-25, said the market fully priced a quarter-point hike for that meeting and two more in 2027.

Coverage of the release stops at the economy. CNBC reports the inflation figures and the Fed pricing and offers no guidance to a business. The explainers a finance team finds when it searches for the method, such as AdaptCFO's revenue bridge guide from 2025-10-01 and Hunting Alice's price volume mix guide from 2026-07-18, give the formulas and a widget or coffee-shop example. None of them starts where a CFO starts this week: three QuickBooks files, a November board package due in days, a 2027 budget that says revenue plus 4 percent with no unit assumption behind it, and a national report saying units are not growing. The rest of this article is that procedure.

The bridge: three effects and one tie-out

Price volume mix analysis splits the change in revenue between two periods into the part that came from charging a different price, the part that came from selling a different quantity, and the part that came from selling a different assortment. Revenue is a flow, so the bridge compares two flows, October 2025 against October 2026 here, and every effect carries the sign of the revenue change it explains: a price increase is positive, a unit decline is negative.

Three conventions keep the result stable. Price effect for each item is the change in net realized price times current-period quantity: (P1 minus P0) times Q1. Net realized price is net revenue divided by units, so discounts, promotions, and credit memos land in the price effect, not in volume. Volume effect is the change in total quantity at the base period's average price and base period mix: (total Q1 minus total Q0) times average P0. Mix effect is what remains of the item-level volume math after the constant-mix volume is removed: for each item, (Q1 minus Q0 times the ratio of total Q1 to total Q0) times P0, summed. The three effects add to the total revenue change to the dollar. If they don't, something in the extract is wrong, and the mix term is not allowed to absorb it.

The unit has to exist. For a distributor it is units shipped by item. For a services firm it is billable hours or jobs. For a subscription business it is active subscriptions, and the revenue is what was recognized in the month, not what was billed, because billings sit in deferred revenue on the balance sheet until earned. Sales tax never enters: it is a liability collected for the state. Intercompany sales come out before the group bridge is built, or the group will show volume it never sold to anyone.

Three entities, one October: the walk-through

Call it Harbor Line Group: a wholesale distributor, a field services company, and a direct-to-consumer web store, each in its own QuickBooks Online file, consolidated monthly. The figures are illustrative; the sequence is the point.

Step one: pull invoice lines, not the profit and loss

From each file the controller runs the sales by product or service detail report for October 2025 and October 2026, filtered to invoices, sales receipts, and credit memos, with quantity, rate, amount, item, and class on every line. Credit memos carry negative quantity and amount. Sales tax lines are excluded. For the services company the quantity column is hours. For the web store the e-commerce sync posts one sales receipt per order, so quantity is orders and rate is the net order value after the promotion code. Intercompany invoices between the distributor and the web store are tagged and removed from the group view.

Step two: build each entity's bridge

The distributor sold two lines. Line A moved 10,000 units at $20.00 in October 2025 and 9,400 units at $21.50 in October 2026. Line B moved 4,000 units at $50.00 and then 4,200 at $52.00. Revenue went from $400,000 to $420,500, up 5.1 percent, while total units fell from 14,000 to 13,600. Price effect: $1.50 times 9,400 plus $2.00 times 4,200, or $22,500. Volume effect at base price and base mix: 400 fewer units times the base average of $28.57, or minus $11,429. Mix effect: Line B's share rose, and at base prices that is worth $9,429. The three sum to $20,500, which ties to the ledger.

The services company billed 6,000 hours at $95 in October 2025 and 5,700 hours at $103 in October 2026. Revenue rose from $570,000 to $587,100, up 3.0 percent. Price effect: $8 times 5,700, or $45,600. Volume effect: 300 fewer hours times $95, or minus $28,500. A 3 percent revenue gain sits on a 5 percent drop in hours.

The web store took 12,000 orders at a net $42.00 in October 2025 and 12,600 orders at a net $40.50 in October 2026, after a free-shipping promotion. Revenue rose from $504,000 to $510,300, up 1.3 percent. Price effect: minus $1.50 times 12,600, or minus $18,900. Volume effect: 600 more orders times $42.00, or $25,200. This is the only entity that grew units, and it bought them with price.

Step three: read the group number the way BEA reads the economy

Group revenue rose $43,900, or 3.0 percent. Price contributed $49,200, about 3.3 percent of the base. Volume took away $14,729, about 1.0 percent. Mix added $9,429, about 0.6 percent. Put the way the October release puts it: nominal revenue up 3.0 percent, real revenue down about 0.4 percent. The group raised prices a little less than the 3.8 percent economy-wide PCE index and sold fewer units, which is the national pattern in miniature. The board deck that said 'revenue up 3 percent year over year' was true and told the directors nothing they needed.

Step four: give the 2027 revenue budget a volume line

The draft 2027 budget carried group revenue at $18.72 million, up 4 percent on a 2026 run rate of $18.0 million, built as last year plus a growth rate. There was no unit assumption anywhere in the model. Once the October bridge exists, the budget is rebuilt as units times price by entity. The distributor plans units down 2 percent and a 3 percent list price increase effective January 1, with mix held flat: revenue up about 0.9 percent. The services company plans hours flat and a 4 percent rate increase on renewals through the year, averaging 2.5 percent for 2027: revenue up 2.5 percent. The web store plans orders up 4 percent and net order value flat, which means the promotion budget is now a line item: revenue up 4 percent. Weighted by entity, the group comes to about 2.6 percent, not 4. The planned price actions add to about 1.8 percent on average; the 4 percent budget needs about 3.2 percent with the same unit plan. The difference, about $250,000 on $18 million, is price that nobody had approved. The CFO takes two options to the board: price actions that add to 3.2 percent on average, with dates and owners, including ending the web store's free-shipping promotion, or the 2.6 percent budget with the cost plan trimmed to match. A revenue budget with no volume line is a price assumption with no signature.

The cost side of the same budget is a separate exercise. The October producer price index, up 6.5 percent over twelve months, and the December rate decision belong in the cost inflation table by vendor and account, and a floating-rate loan reprices on the day the Fed moves. The revenue bridge decides how much of that cost can be passed through at all: an entity losing units has less pricing room than its revenue growth suggests.

Step five: write the November variance in three numbers

The November close will land in the second week of December, days after the Fed decision. The bridge is rebuilt for November against November 2025 and against the budget month, by entity, in the same template, and the variance commentary reads: price plus X, volume minus Y, mix plus Z, with one sentence per entity on what moved. Trading days are checked first, because November 2026 has one fewer Saturday than November 2025, and a comparison that ignores the calendar reports the calendar as volume. The group page of the board package shows the consolidated bridge; each entity page shows its own, so a director can see that the distributor's price held while its units slipped without opening a QuickBooks file. The consolidated budget versus actual template gets three new columns and loses the one called growth percent.

Time: about two hours per entity for the first bridge, most of it checking the unit column; under an hour a month after that. The alternative was a budget that promised 4 percent, an October that delivered 3 percent of price and no units, and a December board meeting where the directors learned the difference from the Fed before they learned it from the CFO.

Accounting controls for the revenue bridge

Source data: invoice, sales receipt, and credit memo lines for both periods from each entity's file, with item, class or location, quantity, rate, and net amount; the recognized revenue journal for any subscription entity; the intercompany customer list; the trading-day calendar for both months; the dated releases relied on, Personal Income and Outlays for October 2026 published 2026-11-25 and the FOMC minutes released 2026-11-18; and the draft 2027 budget with its growth assumptions.

Calculation: a fixed sequence anyone can rerun. Net realized price per item equals net amount divided by quantity for each period. Price effect equals (P1 minus P0) times Q1 per item, summed. Volume effect equals (total Q1 minus total Q0) times the base-period average price, where average price equals base revenue divided by base units. Mix effect equals the sum over items of (Q1 minus Q0 times total Q1 divided by total Q0) times P0. Price plus volume plus mix equals the revenue change on the ledger for the entity, to the dollar. Group effects are the sum of entity effects after intercompany lines are removed. Budget revenue by entity equals planned units times planned net price, with the mix assumption stated; the group figure is the sum, never a growth rate applied to last year.

Review: a second person ties each entity's base and current revenue in the bridge to the revenue section of that entity's profit and loss for the month; ties unit totals to the warehouse, timesheet, or order system; confirms credit memos and promotions sit in price and not in volume; confirms sales tax and intercompany lines are excluded; checks that items new or discontinued between the periods are shown on their own line rather than forced through the mix formula; and confirms the effects sum to the ledger change with no plug.

Decision: the CFO owns the volume assumption in the budget and signs it. Sales or pricing leadership owns each price action, with an effective date and the list of customers it reaches. The controller owns the bridge template and the tie-out. The board approves a revenue budget that states units and price, and the variance commentary each month reports the three effects rather than a growth percentage.

Limits and common mistakes

The release is national and covers consumers. A business that sells to other businesses sees its demand in order books and in the producer price series, not in PCE. The October real spending decline is less than 0.1 percent, one month, and will be revised on December 23. Harbor Line Group, its entities, and every figure are illustrative. Price volume mix conventions differ: some guides price at base volume rather than current volume, and the mix term changes with the order of the calculation. Pick one convention, write it down, and keep it.

Don't call revenue growth minus an inflation index real growth. Your own price effect is the deflator; the national index is context.

Don't bridge billings. Bridge recognized revenue, and leave deferred revenue on the balance sheet where it belongs.

Don't let discounts and promotions hide in volume. They lower net realized price, and the price effect should say so.

Don't compare calendar months with different trading days without saying so. The calendar is not a customer.

Don't leave intercompany sales in the group bridge. They inflate both price and volume with revenue the group never earned.

Don't budget a growth rate. Budget units and price, by entity, and let the growth rate fall out.

Don't wait for the December meeting to find out what price increase the budget assumes. The board should hear it in November.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the October 2026 Personal Income and Outlays report say about consumer spending?

The Bureau of Economic Analysis reported on November 25, 2026 that current-dollar personal consumption expenditures rose $63.8 billion, or 0.3 percent, in October, with $11.8 billion in goods and $52.1 billion in services. The PCE price index rose 0.3 percent in the month and 3.8 percent from a year earlier, 3.3 percent excluding food and energy, so real spending fell $5.8 billion, less than 0.1 percent. Personal income rose 0.7 percent and the saving rate was 4.1 percent.

What is price volume mix analysis?

Price volume mix analysis splits the change in revenue between two periods into three effects: price, the change in net realized price times current quantity; volume, the change in total quantity at the base period's average price and mix; and mix, the revenue change from selling a different assortment at base prices. The three effects add to the total revenue change. It tells a finance team whether revenue grew because customers paid more, bought more, or bought different things.

Where does the data for price volume mix analysis come from in QuickBooks Online?

From the sales by product or service detail report for each period, filtered to invoices, sales receipts, and credit memos, with item, class or location, quantity, rate, and net amount on every line. Sales tax lines are excluded because sales tax is a liability, intercompany invoices are removed before the group bridge, and subscription entities use recognized revenue rather than billings. Each entity's bridge is tied to the revenue section of its profit and loss for the month.

Should a 2027 revenue budget include a volume line?

Yes. A budget built as last year plus a growth rate contains an unstated price assumption. Building it as planned units times planned net price by entity makes the volume assumption visible, lets the board approve a price action with a date and an owner, and gives the monthly variance commentary something to compare against. When the October 2026 release shows national real spending flat to down, a budget that assumes unit growth needs a stated reason.

Does the December 2026 Fed meeting change the revenue bridge?

Not the bridge itself, which reports what happened to price, volume, and mix. The FOMC meets December 8 to 9, 2026, the October minutes released November 18 show almost all participants expecting further increases, and a quarter-point hike was fully priced after the October inflation report. A higher rate reprices floating-rate debt and the interest line of the budget on the day it takes effect, and it is one more reason the volume line in the 2027 budget should not assume customers borrow to buy more.

Once each entity's revenue change is three numbers instead of one, the November board package writes itself and the 2027 budget has a volume line someone signed.
